task.title: Font selection and sizing
task.shortdesc: Choose the font family, the size and the face of your text, and control the height of its lines. Put the declarations in rules that select the XML elements that you want to style.

context.p: The element names in the examples, such as chapter and term, are placeholders. Use the names that occur in your XML.

info.p: Use font-family to list the families to try, in order of preference. Separate them with commas and put a name that contains spaces in quotes:

The last name, serif, is a generic family. It is a keyword, so it has no quotes. CSSMedia maps three generic families to the standard fonts of PDF: serif is Times, sans-serif is Helvetica and monospace is Courier. The generic family math is the first font of the fonts folder that has a MATH table, or Times if there is none. The other generic families have no built-in font, so CSSMedia skips them and tries the next family in the list.

CSSMedia finds a family in these places, in this order: the @font-face rules of your stylesheet, the standard fonts of PDF, and the fonts folder that you pass with -f. It never uses the fonts installed in your computer. The next topic explains how to load your fonts.

A family may not have every character of your text. For each character, CSSMedia tries the families of the list in order. If none has the character, it tries Helvetica, Symbol and ZapfDingbats, and then it draws the missing-character glyph of Helvetica. List a family for every script that your documents use.
Every PDF reader has the 14 standard fonts, and CSSMedia includes their metrics. You can name each of the five families:

Times has serifs and Helvetica does not. Courier is monospaced: all its glyphs have the same width. Symbol has symbols, and ZapfDingbats has ornaments. The default font of CSSMedia, which is the font of text with no font-family, is Helvetica. ISO 32000-1, section 9.6.2, defines these fonts.
Use font-size to set the size of the text. The value is a length such as 12pt, a percentage, or a keyword:

An em or a percentage is relative to the font size of the parent element. The keywords larger and smaller make the size larger or smaller than the size of the parent. The keywords from xx-small to xxx-large are absolute sizes, and the initial value is medium.

When a fallback font looks smaller than the preferred font at the same size, use font-size-adjust. It scales the text so that one metric of the font has the same relative size in every font. The metric is ex-height, which is the height of the lowercase letters and is the default, or cap-height, ch-width, ic-width or ic-height. The value is a number, or from-font to use the metric of the first font that is available:
Within a family, CSSMedia chooses the face that best matches three properties, in this order: font-width, font-style and font-weight.

Use font-weight to choose how heavy the letters look. The values are normal, which is 400, bold, which is 700, or a number from 1 to 1000. The values bolder and lighter are relative to the weight of the parent element:

Use font-width to ask for narrower or wider letters. The value is a percentage, where 100% is normal, or a keyword from ultra-condensed, which is 50%, to ultra-expanded, which is 200%. The old name font-stretch is an alias:

Use font-style to ask for upright or slanted letters. The values are normal, italic, and oblique with an optional angle from -90deg to 90deg. If you do not write an angle, it is 14deg. The values left and right ask for an italic or oblique face that slants clockwise or counter-clockwise:
If the family has no face for the weight, width or style that you request, CSSMedia uses the closest face that exists. The next topic explains how a declared face states what it provides.

When a family has no bold or slanted face, CSSMedia can create one. It draws a thin outline around the glyphs to make them bold, and it shears the glyphs to make them slanted. The standard fonts of PDF have bold and slanted faces, so they never need synthesis. CSSMedia can also create small capitals and the superscript and subscript forms that Font variants and features explains.

Use font-synthesis to forbid these faces. The value none forbids all of them. Otherwise list the kinds that you allow: weight, style, small-caps and position. Four properties control one kind each. Their value is auto to allow or none to forbid, and font-synthesis-style also accepts oblique-only, which allows oblique faces but not italic faces:

stepxmp.pre: body { font-synthesis: none; } code { font-synthesis-weight: none; }

info.p: The four longhand properties are font-synthesis-weight, font-synthesis-style, font-synthesis-small-caps and font-synthesis-position.

step.cmd: Use the shorthand and set the line height

info.p: Use font to set several properties in one declaration. Write the optional style, variant, weight and width first, then the size, an optional slash and line height, and the family. The size and the family are required:

stepxmp.pre: chapter { font: italic bold 12pt/1.4 "Noto Serif", serif; }

info.p: The shorthand resets to their initial values all the font properties that you do not write, including the variant and feature properties. To keep them, use separate declarations. The shorthand also accepts the system font keywords caption, icon, menu, message-box, small-caption and status-bar. A PDF has no system fonts, so CSSMedia gives the keyword the system-ui family and the initial values of the other properties.

Use line-height to set the height of the lines. A number multiplies the font size of the element, a length gives the height directly, and a percentage is relative to the font size. The value normal uses the metrics of the font. A number is the best choice, because it adapts when the font size changes:
